item.title: How to get corporate gifting right across multiple cities
item.description:
How to get corporate gifting right across multiple cities
Sending Diwali gifts to a handful of employees or clients is relatively simple. Sending hundreds of gifts to recipients spread across different cities is another matter. Addresses need to be verified, budgets finalized, packaging standard
item.content:encoded:
Sending Diwali gifts to a handful of employees or clients is relatively simple. Sending hundreds of gifts to recipients spread across different cities is another matter. Addresses need to be verified, budgets finalized, packaging standardized and deliveries timed to arrive before the festival. A missed shipment, incorrect address or last-minute change can quickly complicate the exercise.

For businesses managing large-scale Diwali gifting, the key is to plan early, coordinate the details and ensure that every recipient has a consistent experience, regardless of location.

Start with a detailed recipient list

The first step is to organize all recipient information in one place. This should include names, delivery addresses, contact numbers, and any other information required to complete the delivery. For employee gifting, it may also be useful to group recipients according to city or office location. Client and partner lists can be organized separately so that different gifting requirements are easier to manage. Checking the information before placing the order is important. Incorrect or incomplete addresses can create delivery problems, particularly when gifts are being sent to several cities.

Personalize where it matters

Large-scale gifting does not have to feel completely impersonal. Businesses can add small details that make gifts feel more thoughtful. A personalized greeting card, recipient name or company message can add a sense of occasion without making the process significantly more complicated. For key clients or long-term partners, businesses may choose a more customized gift, based on the relationship. The goal is to find the right level of personalization for each recipient group while keeping the overall process manageable.

Use bulk ordering to simplify the process

When a business is managing a large number of recipients, placing individual orders can quickly become time-consuming. Bulk ordering can make the process more organized, particularly when the same or similar gifts are being sent to multiple locations. A single gifting plan can cover product selection, quantities, packaging, and delivery requirements. This also makes it easier for the internal team to monitor the overall budget and track the progress of the campaign. Businesses planning corporate Diwali gifts can also establish recipient categories in advance, making it easier to decide which gift goes to which group.

Keep packaging consistent

Packaging plays an important role in professional Diwali gifting. When gifts are being sent to different cities, consistent packaging can create a unified brand experience. The same box style, colour scheme, greeting card or branding element can be used across the entire order. This helps ensure that recipients receive gifts that feel like part of the same Diwali campaign, even if they are in different locations. Packaging should also be practical enough to protect the contents during transportation. Fragile products or items sensitive to heat may need additional consideration.

Set a clear budget

Diwali gifting costs can increase quickly when the recipient list is large. Setting a budget before selecting products helps businesses narrow down suitable options. The budget can be divided by recipient category. For example, employee gifts may have one price range, while client or business-partner gifts may have another. It is also useful to account for packaging, delivery, and personalization costs rather than looking only at the product price.

Track every shipment

Once the Diwali gifts are ordered, tracking becomes one of the most important parts of the process. A simple tracking sheet can include the recipient, city, order status, and delivery status. This allows the business team to quickly identify delayed or unsuccessful deliveries and take action where required. For larger gifting programmes, having one person or team responsible for monitoring the campaign can make communication much easier. It also prevents different departments from working with separate or outdated recipient lists.

Decide what the gift should include

The next step is deciding what will go into the Diwali gift. Businesses have several options, from traditional sweets and dry fruits to chocolates, snacks, candles and curated hampers. The choice can depend on the recipient group. Employee gifts may follow one format, while important client or partner gifts may have a different product mix. A consistent selection across cities can make large-scale gifting easier to coordinate. At the same time, businesses can create different categories of gifts based on the relationship with each recipient. This balance can help maintain consistency without making every gift identical.

Plan for different delivery locations

Sending gifts across multiple cities requires attention to delivery coverage and timelines. Businesses should confirm whether the selected gifting provider can deliver to all the required locations and understand how long each delivery may take. This becomes especially important during Diwali because demand for gifting and delivery services can increase significantly around the festival. Businesses can group orders by city and create a delivery schedule before placing them. This makes it easier to track which gifts have been dispatched, which are in transit, and which have already reached the recipients.

Start planning before the festive rush

One of the easiest ways to make multi-city Diwali gifting smoother is to start early. Early planning gives businesses more time to finalize recipient details, compare gifting options, approve designs, and schedule deliveries. It also leaves room to handle unexpected issues, such as an incorrect address or a product becoming unavailable. Waiting until the last few days can limit the available options and put additional pressure on both the business team and the delivery network.

Making multi-city Diwali gifting easier

Diwali gifting across several cities requires more planning than a small personal gifting exercise, but the process becomes manageable when it is treated as a structured campaign. A clear recipient database, suitable gifts, consistent packaging, planned delivery schedules, and proper tracking can help businesses coordinate gifting across locations. The aim is not simply to send gifts to as many people as possible. It is to create a consistent and thoughtful festive experience, even when recipients are spread across different cities.

item.title: Why better data could be the key to AI-driven food R&D
item.description: As food companies navigate increasingly complex product development and safety requirements, connected data and generative AI could help scientists make better-informed decisions, reduce manual work and identify potential risks earlier.
item.content:encoded:
Picture a product developer creating a plant-based protein drink for three different markets. The product concept is clear; the information needed to build it is not. Supplier specifications are locked inside PDFs. Trial results sit in spreadsheets. Regulatory requirements arrive by email. Even a single ingredient can carry a different name in each document: “haldi” in one file, “turmeric” in another and “Curcuma longa” in a regulatory note. None of these files is wrong. The problem is that the information is scattered.

As a result, the developer spends more time searching, matching, and verifying data than working on the product itself. This has become common across food, beverage, and wellness R&D. Creating a product is no longer only about getting the taste and texture right. It is also about managing and connecting an ever-growing volume of data.

Why the data load keeps growing

Food product development is becoming more complex, and food safety sits at the centre of that complexity. The World Health Organization’s 2026 estimates, which cover 42 foodborne hazards, found that unsafe food caused an estimated 866 million illnesses and 1.5 million deaths worldwide in 2021. Chemical hazards accounted for 73% of these deaths, with inorganic arsenic and lead alone responsible for 42% and 31% of chemical-related deaths, respectively. The economic toll is just as stark: WHO puts the productivity lost to foodborne disease at $310 billion in 2021.

The challenge multiplies when companies develop products for several markets at once. Each market brings its own allergen rules, contaminant limits, permitted claims and labelling norms, and the ingredients themselves vary. In wellness products, for instance, the composition of a botanical can shift with its source, harvest season and processing. With every new ingredient, supplier and market, the volume of information that must be checked and connected keeps growing.

Giving data a common language

The answer is not another database. It is a shared vocabulary with the relationships built in, which is exactly what an ontology provides. FoodOn, an open food ontology described in npj Science of Food in 2018, was created to tackle a familiar problem: food data siloed across disparate languages and data dictionaries. Still actively maintained, it now contains tens of thousands of classes covering food products, their plant and animal sources, and the processes used to make them.

Inside a company, the principle is simple. Turmeric is turmeric, whatever name appears in a spreadsheet, supplier document or regulatory file. An ontology can link that one ingredient to its specification, supplier lot, test results, claims and market requirements. Instead of merely matching keywords across thousands of documents, AI can recognise that different names refer to the same ingredient and connect it to the details that matter. A question such as “Which approved ingredients could breach the lead limit in Market B?” then shifts from a slow, manual exercise to a rapid, data-driven check.

Where GenAI fits

Generative AI can read supplier documents, scan scientific literature, suggest alternative ingredients and help draft R&D reports. But when information is fragmented, AI can miss important connections or produce answers that are hard to verify. In some cases, it may generate details that sound plausible but are simply not true.

An ontology can help address this by grounding GenAI in structured, connected facts. Rather than guessing from loose text, the model can draw on linked information about an ingredient, its supplier, its test history, the rules it must satisfy and the claims made for it, and show where each answer came from. This makes AI outputs easier to check and, ultimately, easier to trust. The ontology provides the map; GenAI makes that map usable.

Safety built in, not bolted on

In most organisations, even when quality checks run throughout development, some risks only become visible late, once a finished batch reaches the lab. Connected data can bring those risks into view at the design stage. If a developer selects a rice-based protein, the system can flag a potential inorganic arsenic risk well before a pilot batch is made, since rice absorbs arsenic from soil and water more readily than most other cereals. If a recipe changes, implications for allergens and cross-contact can surface immediately. This matters because many foodborne illnesses are preventable, and catching risks upstream reduces rework, delays and costly product recalls.

The scientist stays in the loop

AI can produce a formulation that is confident and wrong. It cannot taste bitterness, feel grittiness or predict how a blend will behave after months in a humid warehouse.

Consider one high-protein beverage project. The AI recommended a pea protein isolate with added calcium and a stabiliser system, a combination that met every target for protein, nutrition and ingredient constraints on paper. In the lab, however, the proteins aggregated after heat processing, leading to visible settling and a chalky mouthfeel. The team had to rework the mineral load and the stabiliser system before the formulation could move forward.

The working rule is simple: AI proposes; scientists decide. Every suggestion should trace back to a source, be tested at the bench and be signed off by a qualified person. This matters most in safety and regulatory decisions, where accountability cannot be delegated to software.

What comes next

The future of food R&D is not about robot chefs. It is about shorter development cycles, because no one has to waste time hunting for information. It is about keeping institutional knowledge within the organisation, even after a scientist moves on. And it is about building safety and compliance into a product from day one, rather than adding them at the end.

The messy, unglamorous work of cleaning, naming and connecting data will decide who gets real value from AI. The advantage may not go to the company with the most powerful model, but to the one whose data both people and machines can understand.


(Vicky Dodani is the Co-founder of Agrizy)

item.title: Lessons in Chemistry: 5 Takeaways from Bonnie Garmus’ Novel
item.description: Discover five powerful lessons from Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus about equality, ambition, independent thinking, and self-worth.
item.content:encoded:
Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus is a thought-provoking novel about ambition, gender inequality, motherhood, and the courage to challenge social expectations.

Set in the 1960s, the story follows Elizabeth Zott, a brilliant chemist whose professional ambitions are constantly challenged by a society that believes women belong in the kitchen rather than the laboratory.

When Elizabeth unexpectedly becomes the host of a cooking television show, she uses the opportunity to teach more than recipes. Through science, she encourages women to think independently, question established beliefs, and recognise their own abilities.

The novel offers several meaningful lessons about self-worth, equality, and the importance of refusing to let society define who we can become.

5 Powerful ideas in Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus

1. Never let society define your potential

One of the most important lessons in Lessons in Chemistry is that your potential should never be determined by society's expectations.

Elizabeth Zott is an exceptionally talented scientist, but she faces discrimination because she is a woman working in a male-dominated field. Instead of being judged solely on her knowledge and abilities, she repeatedly encounters people who underestimate her because of her gender.

Her experiences highlight how social stereotypes can prevent talented individuals from reaching their full potential. Elizabeth refuses to accept these limitations as the truth about herself. She continues pursuing her interests and challenges the assumptions that attempt to hold her back.

The lesson is simple: your abilities are not limited by what others believe you can achieve. Whether in your career, education, or personal life, you deserve the opportunity to explore your potential without being restricted by outdated expectations.

2. Question everything instead of accepting it blindly

Elizabeth approaches life with the curiosity of a scientist. She believes in examining evidence, asking questions, and understanding why things happen rather than accepting conventional wisdom without thinking.

This mindset becomes particularly important when she begins hosting her cooking show, Supper at Six. Although the programme is designed around cooking, Elizabeth introduces scientific explanations and encourages her audience to understand the processes behind everyday tasks.

Her approach transforms an ordinary television show into an opportunity for women to learn, think critically, and develop confidence in their own intelligence.

The novel reminds readers that questioning established ideas is not necessarily an act of rebellion. Sometimes, it is the first step towards progress.

In everyday life, this means examining the beliefs we inherit, questioning unfair traditions, and making decisions based on reason rather than fear of judgement. Independent thinking allows us to recognise when something needs to change.

3. Women deserve equal opportunities and respect

Gender inequality is a central theme throughout Lessons in Chemistry. Elizabeth encounters professional discrimination, unequal treatment, and assumptions about what women should do with their lives.

Her experiences reflect a broader social problem: women's achievements have often been overlooked simply because they do not fit traditional expectations.

Through Elizabeth's journey, Bonnie Garmus illustrates how exhausting it can be to prove one's competence in an environment where others are unwilling to offer equal opportunities. Elizabeth must work harder to have her knowledge recognised, even when her qualifications speak for themselves.

However, the novel also demonstrates the importance of women supporting one another and recognising their shared potential.

The lesson extends beyond the workplace. Equality means respecting women's choices, valuing their contributions, and allowing them to pursue careers and ambitions without being forced into predefined roles.

A person's capabilities should determine their opportunities, not their gender.

Also Read
7 Things to Accept About Yourself Before You Turn 30

4. Intelligence and confidence can change the way people think

Elizabeth's transformation into a television personality demonstrates that knowledge can be a powerful tool for challenging social attitudes.

Rather than abandoning her scientific background to fit the expectations of a cooking show, she brings science into the kitchen. She explains cooking through chemistry and treats her viewers as intelligent individuals capable of understanding complex ideas.

Her approach challenges the assumption that domestic responsibilities and intellectual pursuits must exist separately. It also gives women a platform to engage with science in a way that traditional institutions have often denied them.

Elizabeth's confidence is not about proving that she is better than everyone else. It comes from knowing the value of her knowledge and refusing to make herself smaller to satisfy other people's expectations.

This lesson encourages readers to embrace their expertise, communicate their ideas clearly, and trust their ability to make a difference.

Sometimes, changing people's perspectives begins with one person who is willing to challenge the familiar and present a different way of thinking.

5. Family and personal identity can exist beyond traditional roles

Another meaningful lesson from Lessons in Chemistry is that people should be allowed to define family and identity on their own terms.

Elizabeth's life challenges conventional ideas about motherhood, relationships, and women's responsibilities. Her experiences show that being a mother does not mean abandoning one's ambitions, just as pursuing a career does not make someone less capable of caring for a family.

The novel explores how people navigate grief, parenthood, relationships, and the expectations placed upon them. It presents a more nuanced understanding of what it means to build a fulfilling life.

Elizabeth refuses to accept that she must choose between being intellectually ambitious and being a devoted parent. Instead, she creates a life that reflects her circumstances, values, and priorities.

For readers, the lesson is that there is no single formula for a meaningful life. People have different ambitions, responsibilities, and definitions of happiness.

Rather than measuring ourselves against conventional milestones, we can focus on building lives that align with our own values and allow us to grow.

Final thoughts

Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus is more than a novel about a scientist navigating a world that underestimates her. It is a story about challenging inequality, embracing curiosity, and refusing to let other people's assumptions determine your future.

Through Elizabeth Zott's experiences, readers are reminded that intelligence deserves recognition, women deserve equal opportunities, and personal ambition should not be sacrificed to satisfy society's expectations.

The five lessons from the book encourage us to question outdated beliefs, trust our abilities, and create lives that reflect who we truly are. Whether you are navigating your career, questioning social norms, or discovering your own identity, Elizabeth's journey offers a powerful reminder that you do not have to fit into someone else's definition of success.

Ultimately, Lessons in Chemistry encourages readers to approach life with curiosity, courage, and the confidence to challenge what they have been told is possible.

item.title: ‘Cope harder’: Vaishnaw defends India's iPhone PLI scheme
item.description: “Cope harder,” says Ashwini Vaishnaw as he defends India’s manufacturing model, citing Rs 3 lakh crore in GST collections, government incentives and jobs created through electronics production.
item.content:encoded:
Assembling iPhones makes great headlines for India. Owning the supply chain is where the real power lies.

Apple assembled around 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, a 53% increase from 36 million units in 2024. The country now accounts for about a quarter of Apple's global iPhone output, according to a Bloomberg report.

The growth has strengthened India's position as an alternative manufacturing base to China.

While skeptics question whether snapping together foreign components delivers true high-tech independence, the government points to ₹3.25 lakh crore in tax collections and 12 lakh new jobs as proof that the PLI scheme is already paying off handsomely.

Vaishnaw counters criticism with tax and employment figures

The debate intensified after a Bloomberg Opinion video questioned whether India should replicate China's manufacturing model. It highlighted India's dependence on imported components and the cost of government subsidies supporting phone production.

Union Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw responded on X on October 27, defending the government's Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for mobile manufacturing.

According to the figures he shared, the government had paid Rs 19,000 crore in incentives, while direct tax collections reached Rs 25,000 crore. The sector had also generated Rs 3 lakh crore in Goods and Services Tax (GST) collections.

Mobile PLI stats as follows:
Government incentive paid: Rs 19,000 Cr.
Direct tax collected: Rs 25,000 Cr.
GST collected: Rs 3,00,000 Cr.
Electronics manufacturing employs 25 Lakh people; mobile manufacturing alone employs 12 Lakh.

Cope harder!! https://t.co/G3bDU6ldGg

— Ashwini Vaishnaw (@AshwiniVaishnaw) October 27, 2026

Vaishnaw also cited employment figures, saying electronics manufacturing supported 25 lakh jobs, including 12 lakh in mobile phone manufacturing.

He ended his post with the pointed remark, “Cope harder!!” The figures form the government's case for continuing to support domestic manufacturing. However, tax collections and job creation are only part of the discussion.

India's iPhone growth comes with a supply chain challenge

India's expanding role in Apple's manufacturing network is a significant development. In 2025, the country assembled around 55 million iPhones, up from 36 million in 2024.

Apple also began assembling all variants of its iPhone 17 line-up in India, including the Pro and Pro Max models, according to The Times of India.

Yet assembling a finished product is different from manufacturing all its components locally. India continues to depend on imports for several critical parts, including processors, memory chips, displays, camera lenses and batteries.

This matters because the economic value generated by manufacturing depends partly on how much of the supply chain operates within the country. Greater domestic production of components could help Indian suppliers capture more value while reducing reliance on overseas manufacturers.

The next test is building more of the iPhone in India

The government's manufacturing push now faces a more demanding test: turning higher production volumes into a deeper domestic electronics ecosystem.

That means expanding local component manufacturing, bringing more suppliers into the country and strengthening research and design capabilities. These steps could help India progress beyond final assembly and establish a more substantial presence in global electronics supply chains.

India's iPhone production growth demonstrates that the country can attract large-scale manufacturing. Whether that translates into lasting economic gains will depend on its ability to build more of the technology and supply chain behind each device.

item.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (October 28, 2026)
item.description: YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Wednesday, October 28, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
From Jio Platforms making a strong debut on the National Stock Exchange on Wednesday with its shares gaining 21.3% over the issue price of Rs 1,119 apiece, to AI that can generate almost anything we ask for, here are the latest developments across sectors.

Featured Stories

When content becomes infinite, what makes people pay attention?

We are living in a world where content is no longer scarce. There is more news, more videos, more creators, and, AI that can generate almost anything we ask for. But this abundance brings a new challenge: when everyone is creating content, how do you get someone to stop scrolling, pay attention, and come back?

On the sidelines of TechSparks 2026, Avinash Mudaliar, Co-founder and CEO of HT Media Labs and the creator of Saregama Carvaan; Deepit Purkayastha, Co-founder and CEO of Inshorts; and GSN Aditya, COO of Eloelo Group, came together for a discussion titled The Format Is the Product: When Content Becomes Infinite.

Read more

Latest News

Jio Platforms makes strong market debut, lists on NSE with a gain of 21.3%

Jio Platforms made a strong debut on the National Stock Exchange on Wednesday with its shares gaining 21.3% over the issue price of Rs 1,119 apiece, resulting in a market capitalisation of Rs 12.5 lakh crore.

The share opened at Rs 1,358 and reached an intraday high of Rs 1,374.50. It was trading at Rs 1,366.60 at 11:41 am with a market capitalisation of Rs 12,58,045.70 crore.

Jio Platforms' Rs 30,213-crore IPO received an overwhelming response from investors. It was oversubscribed in less than two hours on opening day, and closed with a 22X oversubscription.

Read more

Funding News

Healthy snack brand Troovy raises Rs 100 Cr in Series B round led by Fireside Ventures

Troovy, a food and snacks brand, has raised Rs 100 crore in a Series B round of funding led by Fireside Ventures, with participation from Sharrp Ventures and other investors.

The Gurugram-based brand will use the funding for R&D, expanding its manufacturing capacity, and scaling distribution across quick commerce and offline channels, as it looks to launch a wide range of products.

Troovy was founded in 2023 by Mansi Baranwal and Aditya Mukherjee with the goal of providing nutritious food. Its portfolio spans categories such as snacks, sauces and spreads, and millet pasta. It says its vacuum-cooked potato chips have 10-12% oil and high protein, compared with 35-40% oil in mainstream chips. It also promises clean-label ketchups and seasonings without synthetic additives or preservatives.

Read more

Other News

QwikBuild raises $2.3M in pre-seed funding, enters Japan through JV

Bengaluru-based enterprise AI startup QwikBuild has raised $2.3 million in pre-seed funding from Globalway Inc, Blume Ventures, Marsshot, DeVC and angel investors, including Groww founder Lalit Keshre and Cure.fit founder Ankit Nagori. 

The company also announced a joint venture with publicly listed Japanese firm Globalway to enter Japan’s enterprise market. QwikBuild uses autonomous AI agents to build bespoke enterprise software in days, enabling businesses to automate workflows, modernise legacy systems and integrate applications with existing platforms such as SAP and Salesforce. The startup currently serves enterprises across India, the US and Singapore.

PhonePe rebrands Indus Appstore, targets digital goods market with 200 million devices

PhonePe has rebranded its homegrown app marketplace, Indus Appstore, as PhonePe Appstore, as it expands into digital goods and services. The platform is available on more than 200 million devices through original equipment manufacturer (OEM) partnerships, with Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar, Karnataka and Telangana among its top markets. 

Alongside apps and games, users can access gift cards and digital top-ups, with gaming top-ups scheduled to launch first. PhonePe has also introduced phonepeappstore.com, a webstore for discovering and purchasing digital products through browsers. The platform aims to offer developers alternative distribution and monetisation opportunities through payments, advertising and digital sales.

ixigo co-founder Rajnish Kumar launches Rs 1 crore fund to back IIT Kanpur startups

ixigo co-founder and Group Co-CEO Rajnish Kumar has launched the Rs 1 crore Made in Fire Fund to support technology-led startups founded by graduating IIT Kanpur students. Beginning with the Class of 2026, the initiative will select 10 startups per batch, offering each Rs 10 lakh in non-dilutive prototype funding. 

Beyond capital, founders will receive mentorship from Kumar, ixigo’s leadership team and its wider entrepreneur network, alongside product reviews, go-to-market guidance, hiring support and investor introductions. The fund will prioritise founder conviction, customer understanding and execution over pitch decks, backing ventures across AI, SaaS, deep tech, mobility, healthcare and other technology sectors.

CHOSEN Extends Series A with Backing from Wellbeing Nutrition Founders

CHOSEN, India's first exposome-based dermocosmetic brand, has extended its Series A round with investment from Wellbeing Nutrition founders Avnish Chhabria and Saurabh Kapoor, joining Fireside Ventures, L'Oréal's BOLD, and Alkemi Growth Capital. The fresh capital will strengthen R&D, expand the formulation pipeline across topicals and nutraceuticals, and fund a dermatologist-led Centre of Excellence. 

Founded in 2020 by Dr Renita Rajan, the Chennai-based brand formulates melanin-rich Indian skin, targeting pigmentation, texture, contour and hair ageing. It offers over 50 products prescribed by more than 2,000 doctors, and raised a $5 million Series A in May 2026.

Bellatrix Aerospace appoints Kiran U as CFO to drive growth and international expansion

Bengaluru-based in-space mobility company Bellatrix Aerospace has appointed Kiran U as its Chief Financial Officer (CFO) to lead its financial strategy and support business expansion. A Chartered Accountant and Company Secretary, Kiran brings over 17 years of experience across financial planning, treasury, capital raising, taxation, audit and investor relations. 

In his new role, he will focus on capital efficiency, funding diversification, financial discipline and operational scalability as the company pursues international opportunities and expands its commercial pipeline. Bellatrix Aerospace develops in-space propulsion technologies, including Arka Hall Effect Thrusters and Rudra Green Propulsion Systems, for satellite and space missions.

PB Money secures SEBI licence to expand retail access to bonds

PB Money, an investment platform strategically partnered with Paisabazaar, has received a Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) licence as an Online Bond Platform Provider (OBPP). The licence allows the platform to manage the entire bond investment journey, covering investor onboarding, KYC, bond discovery, order placement, payments and post-investment servicing. 

Through its partnership with Paisabazaar, PB Money aims to reach a wider consumer base and simplify access to fixed-income products. Investors can compare bonds based on parameters such as yield, credit rating and investment amount, helping them evaluate options and diversify their portfolios."

PhysicsWallah’s School of Startups partners with DPIIT to support 25,000 startups

PhysicsWallah’s School of Startups (PW SoS) has partnered with the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) under a two-year agreement to support 25,000 early-stage startups across India. The initiative will focus on entrepreneurs in Tier-II and Tier-III cities and rural areas, offering training, mentorship, incubation, seed funding and investor access.

Programmes include PW UDYAMI, a 90-day online course with one year of mentorship, and a six-month DeepTech Accelerator. The partnership will also support prototype development, corporate pilot projects and growth-stage funding readiness, aiming to strengthen regional entrepreneurship and innovation.

Read more

Let’s Game Now raises Rs 30 Cr from Anand Mahindra and other investors

Let’s Game Now, an Indian gaming and esports company, has closed a Rs 30 crore investment round backed by Anand Mahindra, Bestvantage Investments and a UAE-based family office. The company will use the funding to accelerate the development of the Indian Super Gaming League (ISGL), a franchise-based competition combining gaming, sports, entertainment and technology.

The league has also received backing from actors Ranveer Singh and Abhishek Bachchan. Let’s Game Now claims a community of over 1.4 million members and has organised more than 2,000 events. Bestvantage Investments advised the company exclusively on the investment round.

Oracle, Snowflake bring AI Data Cloud to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure

Oracle and Snowflake have announced that Snowflake AI Data Cloud will be available as a native, first-party service on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), expanding options for enterprises seeking to use their data for artificial intelligence and analytics. Customers will be able to purchase, provision and consume the service directly through Oracle, with unified pricing and billing.

They can also use Oracle Universal Credits, simplifying procurement and enabling them to draw on existing cloud commitments. The integration is designed to bring Snowflake’s analytics and AI capabilities closer to enterprise data held across Oracle services, including Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications, NetSuite and Oracle databases.

HCLTech launches AI-powered nano GCC offering with AWS

HCLTech has launched an AI-powered nano Global Capability Centre (GCC) offering built on Amazon Web Services (AWS), aimed at helping enterprises transition from AI experimentation to business outcomes. Part of its GCC 360 solution suite, the model combines HCLTech’s advisory expertise and AI platforms, including AI Force, with AWS infrastructure and agentic AI services.

The offering targets established GCCs seeking AI-led transformation and mid-market companies looking to enter new geographies with lower risk. It focuses on compact, product-centric teams, AI-enabled workflows, autonomous IT operations, engineering, data analytics and intelligent business operations.

BonV Aero completes high-altitude logistics drone trials

Bhubaneswar-based uncrewed aerial systems manufacturer BonV Aero has completed fleet testing of its logistics drones across remote, high-altitude locations, demonstrating payload transport at elevations ranging from 10,500 to 16,500 feet. The trials involved carrying a 32-kg payload and evaluated the performance of heavy-payload unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in challenging operating conditions.

The latest trials build on the company’s earlier achievement of lifting 30 kg to 19,024 feet at Umling La in Ladakh in 2023. It has also supplied 45 heavy-payload UAVs to the Indian Army’s Eastern Command.

Vashi Integrated Solutions plans 22 solar marts across 10 states

Vashi Integrated Solutions plans to establish 22 Vashi Mart outlets across 10 states by FY 2026-27 to improve access to solar equipment and installation essentials for rooftop solar installers. The initiative aims to address procurement challenges, particularly in Tier 2 and Tier 3 markets, by bringing inventory and technical support closer to project locations.

The first phase will cover Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Kerala, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Assam, Uttarakhand and Odisha. The outlets will primarily serve residential rooftop solar installations, while also supporting smaller commercial and industrial projects.

Freshworks acquires Israeli company Robusta Dev

Freshworks, the Nasdaq listed SaaS company has acquired Israeli firm Robusta Dev Ltd  for an undisclosed value. Robusta is a developer of an open source project monitoring platform.

A statement from Freshworks said this acquisition strengthens its capabilities in the segments of incident management and IT operations. It further added it bridges the gap between deep diagnostic intelligence, IT service management, and modern incident orchestration powered by platforms like FireHydrant. 

"Our technology lets AI Agents do that effectively in large enterprise environments, where there are so many raw events that investigating each one individually would be exorbitant from a token cost perspective. We're incredibly excited to join Freshworks, which gives us the scale and platform to bring that experience to engineering teams everywhere, while keeping humans firmly in control of decisions that touch production," said Natan Yellin, co-founder and CEO of Robusta.

Freshworks said the combined entity will bring its AI-powered incident intelligence capabilities into Freshservice workflows while deepening interoperability with incident response platforms like FireHydrant.

The statement said the technology platform of Robusta is optimised for large scale production environments where it covers diagnosis, treatment and prevention.

item.title: ‘Keep learning, keep adapting’: Priyank Kharge tells IT professionals to stay ahead of AI
item.description: Priyank Kharge urges IT professionals to adapt to AI, upgrade their skills and prepare for changing industry needs through initiatives like Nipuna Karnataka.
item.content:encoded:
If there’s one rule for surviving the AI tech shift, it’s that your learning curve can never plateau.

As artificial intelligence reshapes industries and job requirements, IT professionals must keep upgrading their skills and adapting to changing business needs, said Karnataka IT Minister Priyank Kharge on Tuesday.

Speaking at the inauguration of RSM US Integrated Services India Private Limited’s new office at Manyata Tech Park in Bengaluru on October 28, Kharge said the pace of AI adoption was creating uncertainty around future roles, making continuous learning essential for professionals.

“AI is one of the most disruptive technologies we have seen, and the speed and scale at which it is being adopted are unprecedented,” he said.

While predicting exactly how jobs and skill requirements will evolve remains difficult, Kharge said professionals must focus on building capabilities that remain relevant to industry and global markets.

“The opportunity lies in our ability to keep learning, adapt quickly and build capabilities that remain relevant to industry and global markets,” he added.

Karnataka’s talent pool keeps global businesses interested

Priyank Kharge also highlighted Karnataka’s talent pool as a key factor in attracting global businesses and Global Capability Centres (GCCs), which handle specialised business and technology operations for multinational companies.

“We have not seen a talent pool as agile as Karnataka’s, one that is ready to unlearn, relearn and be deployed at scale,” he said.

The minister credited the state’s workforce alongside its policies and infrastructure for helping attract investment. He pointed to Bengaluru’s Outer Ring Road (ORR), where approximately 800,000 people work along a 9-km stretch, describing it as one of the world’s most densely concentrated talent pools.

He added that Karnataka would continue strengthening its infrastructure while building on its workforce advantage to attract investment and support increasingly specialised, high-value work.

Nipuna Karnataka puts industry needs at the centre

To help workers prepare for evolving job requirements, Kharge highlighted Nipuna Karnataka, the state’s industry-led skilling initiative.

The programme brings industry partners into the training process, allowing companies to identify the capabilities they need and help shape relevant curricula. The government and industry then work together to prepare candidates for emerging roles.

Under the model, government support for eligible training costs is linked to employability and employment outcomes. The aim is to ensure training responds to actual hiring needs rather than leaving candidates with skills that employers may not require.

Since AI reshapes how businesses operate, the minister stressed the importance of closer industry participation in identifying emerging skill gaps and preparing the workforce accordingly.

Karnataka’s ability to stay competitive will depend on how well its workforce keeps pace with changing technology. As AI changes job roles and the skills employers look for, continuous learning could prove just as important as technical expertise in helping professionals stay relevant.

item.title: When content becomes infinite, what makes people pay attention?
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, leaders from HT Media Labs, Inshorts, and Eloelo Group discuss why credibility, human creativity, and audience-first formats will matter as content creation scales.
item.content:encoded:
We are living in a world where content is no longer scarce. There is more news, more videos, more creators, and, AI that can generate almost anything we ask for. But this abundance brings a new challenge: when everyone is creating content, how do you get someone to stop scrolling, pay attention, and come back?

On the sidelines of TechSparks 2026, Avinash Mudaliar, Co-founder and CEO of HT Media Labs and the creator of Saregama Carvaan; Deepit Purkayastha, Co-founder and CEO of Inshorts; and GSN Aditya, COO of Eloelo Group, came together for a discussion titled The Format Is the Product: When Content Becomes Infinite.

The conversation explored how formats shape the way audiences consume content, what makes a format resonate in an increasingly crowded digital landscape, and why the format itself can be as important as the content it carries.

What is the differentiator in all this: the format, distribution, personalisation or the relationship with the consumer?

“Actually, the four items you mentioned aren't rivals. They are congruent; they co-exist. And all of them need to be married in a particular combination to get a person to come back. Right now, the problem is not content. Content has become infinite. Time has become finite,” said Mudaliar.

He explained that when he was building Carvaan, he had a clear target audience: people who didn't want to open an app, create a playlist, log in, pay, go through the entire rigmarole just to listen, and then go to a search bar and search for a song.

Carvaan put in 5,000 songs in a fully digitised, personalised product, without advertising itself as digital. Instead, it recreated the experience of listening to old-time radio, limiting the choices available and allowing listeners to immerse themselves in the music. With OTT Play, the focus was primarily on personalisation, helping users decide what to watch, where to watch it and how.

Purkayastha said that when he started Inshorts 12 years ago, people were beginning to consume content on smartphones, but no app was truly innovating on how they consumed news and information on these devices.

“Today, people come to us because they want a reliable, factual source of information. They want to stay updated on the world, but they don't want the noise and provocativeness of social media. We are a source reliable enough that they can use it during their digital detox,” he said.

For Eloelo, the micro-drama format unlocked the ability to tell many more stories faster and reach a wider audience. 

“I think people's tastes continue to change, and while there is infinite content, the top 5% is often where most of the eyeballs go. So it comes down to your ability to keep reinventing the story arc, tell new stories, and deliver them through state-of-the-art data science to personalise content so people always see what they want to see,” said Aditya.

The role of AI

There's a general perception that AI can create everything, so what will audiences actually value? 

Purkayastha says that while AI platforms are increasingly meeting consumers’ on-demand information needs, people still want real-time updates.

“AI can't imagine what's happening at TechSparks right now. Someone has to feed it into the system. That is live content generation, and that is news. Summaries and articles are the collateral that emerge from it.

“When an event happens, the question is which sources and distributors will be trusted. Trust becomes the most interesting capital they build, and I think LLM agents will value it too.”

Aditya believes AI will accelerate content creation but cannot replace human creativity. “It's a great enabler for people to tell stories, but I don't think it will substitute for human creativity,” he says, pointing out that despite the money and data invested in Hollywood and Bollywood, no deterministic system can predict whether a story will be a hit.

“People's tastes continuously change, and their expectations change. That can only be solved by human creativity.”

He added that AI would speed up storytelling workflows, while creativity and inspiration would remain human-driven.

Trust and verification

Mudaliar points to trust and verification as key differentiators in an AI-driven content ecosystem.

“There's a very interesting concept we're trying out at HT Tech right now. HT is already a trusted source for most LLMs for India-oriented news and beyond, simply because we've been around for the last 100 years. We take pride in our journalism, and we put out verified stories. We are now building another ecosystem within HT called HT Verify,” he explained.

“For example, our team member here is capturing this event, creating a video out of it that will also be made into social content, and writing maybe 3,000 words on it, written to the schema AI LLMs prefer and made citable by the AI. So you are literally training the AI that this content is not only trustworthy, it's also verified and ready for consumption. That results in your content being cited and picked up, and then transmogrified for the user,” he added.

For Purkayastha, understanding audiences beyond urban India meant identifying a gap in trustworthy local content. When Inshorts began exploring consumption patterns in smaller cities in 2019, as mobile internet use surged following Jio's arrival, the team realised that local news from smaller towns often went unreported.

“We realised that the biggest gap in those markets was that content generation wasn't happening in a trustworthy way,” he says.

The company addressed this gap with Public, a platform featuring verified creators who report on their towns and cities. Launched in 2019, it has since reached about 80 million users.

For Aditya, micro-drama economics have created opportunities to tell stories for more specific audiences rather than chase mass appeal. With lower production costs and shorter turnaround times, creators can experiment with stories rooted in particular regions and communities.

“I no longer have to make storylines that only appeal to a large catchment of people. I can now talk about storylines relevant to, say, a district in Uttar Pradesh, and the P&L still works. So we're now able to tap into Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, each of these,” he said.

Mudaliar believes the industry still has a long way to go in designing products for India's diverse linguistic audiences. Despite the emphasis on building for Bharat, he argues, many products continue to draw inspiration from platforms designed primarily for urban consumers.

“98% of India consumes in a local language. He doesn't know how to search; he doesn't know how to write in English; he's trying. For him, voice search is the first point of contact because he doesn't know how to type. That's why even Google Maps, even your Uber drivers, use voice. So why aren't we building voice-first products for India?” he asked.

item.title: Info Edge’s Hitesh Oberoi to step down as MD and CEO; founder Sanjeev Bikhchandani to take over
item.description: Info Edge CEO Hitesh Oberoi will step down on 2 December 2026 after nearly 27 years, with founder Sanjeev Bikhchandani returning as MD and Group CEO from 3 December, subject to shareholder approval.
item.content:encoded:
Hitesh Oberoi, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Info Edge, will step down from his full-time executive role on December 2, 2026, after nearly 27 years with the company, including more than 16 years as MD. The parent of Naukri.com announced the leadership change alongside its second-quarter FY27 results.

Sanjeev Bikhchandani, the founder of Info Edge, will take over as Executive Vice Chairman, Managing Director and Group CEO from December 3, 2026, subject to shareholder approval. The move will see Bikhchandani return to an active management role after serving as Executive Vice Chairman. According to the company's regulatory filing, his term will run until April 26, 2031.

Oberoi, however, will continue to be associated with the company. Subject to shareholder approval, he will remain on its board as a Non-Executive, Non-Independent Director. Info Edge said he had chosen to step back from his full-time executive role to devote more time to education, entrepreneurship, institution building, investing and philanthropy, while spending more time with his family.

In a statement, Oberoi said that after nearly 27 years, he felt it was the right time to begin transitioning out of his full-time operating role. He added that he would miss the colleagues and teams who had made those years special. Bikhchandani said the two had built Info Edge together over more than 27 years.

Oberoi's tenure spans much of Info Edge's growth. According to a report citing the company's filing, its market capitalisation increased from Rs 2,500 crore to Rs 80,000 crore during his tenure. Oberoi formally took over as CEO and MD in 2010, when Bikhchandani moved into the role of Executive Vice Chairman. The company said it has a strong institutional foundation, supported by senior leaders who have been with Info Edge for more than 20 years.

Investors will be watching how the leadership change affects Info Edge’s core recruitment business and broader strategy. The move comes after CFO Chintan Thakkar stepped down in November 2025, with co-promoter Ambarish Raghuvanshi taking over as interim CFO.

item.title: Meesho narrows loss by 68% while revenue rises 34% in Q2 of FY27
item.description: The annual transacting user base of Meesho now stands at 284 million for Meesho and the seller base has grown to 1.13 million.
item.content:encoded:
Ecommerce company Meesho reported a 68% decline in net losses even as revenues rose by 34% on a year-on-year (YoY) basis for the second quarter of FY27.

Meesho reported a net loss of Rs 132.44 crore for the three months ending September, 2026 which is the second quarter of FY27 as compared to Rs 411.36 crore recorded in the similar period a year ago.

Revenue for the second quarter touched Rs 4131.58 crore as compared to Rs 3073.67 crore a year ago.

On the performance of the company, Meesho CEO Vidit Aatrey said, “Our Q2 performance reflects the strength of Meesho's operating model, with NMV (net merchandise value) growing 23% year-on-year to Rs 12,911 crore and annual transacting users reaching 284 million. More consumers are shopping on Meesho, and they are shopping more frequently, even as first-time buyers grew 16% quarter-on-quarter.”

According to the company, annual transacting users grew 21% YoY to 284 million while annual purchase frequency increased 7% YoY to 10.4 transactions per user. Meesho said NMV grew 23% YoY.

Meesho said festive-aligned NMV grew 33% YoY over the 90 days preceding Dussehra. The annual transacting sellers increased 60% YoY to 1.13 million. The e-commerce company said over 4 lakh sellers are now part of its Content Commerce ecosystem, enabling entrepreneurs to reach consumers through creator-led product discovery.

For Meesho, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a big differentiator as it transitions towards an agent-led software development with engineering productivity increasing 171% between March and September 2026 and the number of experiments rising 73%.

It noted that approximately 65% of engineering pods now operate with a single engineer directing AI agents.

“Our focus remains on reinvesting these efficiency gains into better consumer and seller experiences, accelerating innovation and building a larger, more efficient marketplace that can generate sustainable free cash flow over the long term,” Aatrey said.

Meesho said as of September 30, 2026, it had a cash balance of Rs 7,048 crore, providing flexibility to pursue long-term growth opportunities while maintaining financial discipline.

item.title: PhysicsWallah partners with DPIIT to support early-stage ventures
item.description: The two-year partnership aims to expand access to training, mentorship, incubation and seed funding for entrepreneurs in smaller cities and rural areas.
item.content:encoded:
PhysicsWallah’s School of Startups (PW SoS) has signed a two-year memorandum of understanding with the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) to support early-stage ventures, particularly in Tier-II and III cities and rural areas. 

The partnership combines training and mentoring with prototype development, incubation, investor access and seed capital.

“Supporting entrepreneurs beyond Tier-I cities is key to building a stronger startup ecosystem in India. Our partnership with PhysicsWallah School of Startups will help grassroots innovators access the resources, mentorship and infrastructure they need to turn their ideas into scalable, job-creating businesses across Bharat,” said Ateesh Kumar Singh, Additional Secretary at DPIIT.

PW SoS, an accredited incubator under Uttar Pradesh’s StartinUP initiative, has programmes for founders at different stages. PW UDYAMI combines 90 days of live online training with a year of mentorship. Aarambh Immersion is a five-day residential programme for prototype development, pitches and networking. The Growth Stage CEO Programme is designed for 200 DPIIT-recognised startups across four hybrid cohorts, while the six-month PW DeepTech Accelerator targets selected ventures. 

The annual National AI Startup Challenge and SeedX are intended to offer proof-of-concept opportunities, corporate pilots and seed investment. The release also cites incubation and seed grants through the StartinUP Business Incubation Centre in Uttar Pradesh.

Rounaq Mustafa, Head of PW SoS, said the aim was to widen access to support. “True empowerment means making knowledge, mentorship and funding accessible to aspiring entrepreneurs across Bharat. Through our partnership with DPIIT and Startup India, PW School of Startups aims to support aspiring founders.”

The tie-up comes as the ecosystem grows and public support expands. DPIIT recently shared that it had recognised 2,50,046 startups across more than 770 districts, with 52% based in non-metro cities. 

The Startup India Seed Fund Scheme had approved Rs 775.67 crore for 4,194 startups through 244 incubators, including 2,356 ventures in Tier-II and III cities. In April, the government notified a Rs 10,000 crore Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0, which channels capital through investment funds rather than directly giving grants to every startup.

Policy is also addressing research-led businesses, which often need longer development periods and more capital. In February, the government extended the recognition window for deeptech startups to 20 years and raised their turnover limit to Rs 300 crore.

Private programmes are specialising too. Google’s 2026 India accelerator selected 20 AI-focused startups from around 2,500 applications for technical and commercialisation support.

item.title: NIT Rourkela scientists develop lead-free light-emitting materials for safer lighting and security applications
item.description: These materials respond to changes in heat and moisture and can have applications in security systems, sensors and lighting technologies.
item.content:encoded:
Researchers from the National Institute of Technology Rourkela (NIT Rourkela), in collaboration with researchers from IIT Guwahati, IIT Bombay, and NISER Bhubaneswar, have developed new materials that can emit different colours of light under ultraviolet (UV) light exposure. 

These materials respond to changes in heat and moisture and can have applications in security systems, sensors, and lighting technologies.

The research investigated bismuth-based compounds as safer alternatives to lead-based photoluminescent materials, which are widely studied for their light-emission properties but raise significant environmental and health concerns because of lead toxicity.

Many materials used for producing light contain lead, which is harmful to human health and the environment. To find a safer alternative, the researchers have investigated bismuth-based compounds, a class of compounds containing both organic and inorganic components, which can offer useful light-emitting properties without relying on lead.

Prof. Saroj L Samal, Associate Professor, said, “The most interesting aspect of this material is its ability to undergo reversible structural transformation in response to heat and moisture, accompanied by change in its light emission properties.”

This discovery has the potential for protecting important documents and products from counterfeiting. For example, special inks containing the developed material can be used on certificates, signatures, and security labels. Their light-emitting properties could be checked under UV light after controlled heating, which could help verify whether an item is genuine.

It could also be useful in humidity sensors. Since its light emission changes with moisture, it may help monitor humidity in food packaging, storage facilities and other places where moisture levels need to be controlled.

Further studies will focus on developing efficient and stimuli-responsive luminescent materials for anti-counterfeiting, improving the sensitivity and reliability of sensors, and optimising the performance of white-light-emitting diodes. These efforts could help translate the findings into practical technologies for optical security, environmental monitoring and cost-effective, energy-efficient lighting.

item.title: Government working to utilise procurement process for promoting startups: DPIIT Secretary
item.description: Elaborating on the move to enhance participation of startups in government procurement, DPIIT Additional Secretary Ateesh Kumar Singh said that there are already certain facilities available in the form of relaxations to the GFR (General Financial Rules).
item.content:encoded:
The government is working to leverage the procurement process to promote startups, a top official of the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade said on Tuesday.

Speaking at the curtain-raiser event for National Startup Awards 6.0, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) Secretary Amardeep Singh Bhatia said that there is a need for more private initiatives to engage with startups and bring them into their supply chain network.

"We are also working with other agencies to see how government procurement can also be better used for promoting startups by providing them with at least early access to demand," he said.

Elaborating on the move to enhance participation of startups in government procurement, DPIIT Additional Secretary Ateesh Kumar Singh said that there are already certain facilities available in the form of relaxations to the GFR (General Financial Rules).

"Also, here are certain circulars which have been put out by various agencies to make the pathway into the government procurement process easier. The partaking of those benefits still remains a challenge. It is there where we are trying to make sure that the offerings are available to them," he said.

Singh said that a lot of problems also occur due to information asymmetry.

"One part of the problem is to tell people what is available. The second part of the problem is partaking in those things. We are also trying to address challenges in our existing system. We are working with various ministries, including the Department of Finance, Public Enterprises and MSME. This is ongoing work and we will come up with a new framework," he said.

He said that the number of startups in the country has grown to over 2.5 lakh, with more than half of them located in tier 3 and smaller towns.

Under the 6th Edition of the National Startup Awards (NSA 6.0), winning startups across the 20 sectoral categories and the two startup-focused special categories will be eligible for a cash prize of Rs 25 lakh per category, subject to the applicable award guidelines.

The student innovator and aspiring entrepreneur award will carry a total prize pool of Rs 25 lakh across four sub-categories.

In addition to monetary recognition, the National Startup Awards seek to facilitate mentorship, investor engagement, market access, industry partnerships and enhanced visibility within India’s startup ecosystem.

The 20 categories will also include three special categories comprising women-led startups, startups from the north-eastern region and student innovators or aspiring entrepreneurs.

item.title: Healthy snack brand Troovy raises Rs 100 Cr in Series B round led by Fireside Ventures
item.description: Gurugram-based Troovy will use the funding for R&D, expanding its manufacturing capacity, and scaling distribution across quick commerce and offline channels.
item.content:encoded:
Troovy, a food and snacks brand, has raised Rs 100 crore in a Series B round of funding led by Fireside Ventures, with participation from Sharrp Ventures and other investors.

The Gurugram-based brand will use the funding for R&D, expanding its manufacturing capacity, and scaling distribution across quick commerce and offline channels, as it looks to launch a wide range of products.

Troovy was founded in 2023 by Mansi Baranwal and Aditya Mukherjee with the goal of providing nutritious food. Its portfolio spans categories such as snacks, sauces and spreads, and millet pasta. It says its vacuum-cooked potato chips have 10-12% oil and high protein, compared with 35-40% oil in mainstream chips. It also promises clean-label ketchups and seasonings without synthetic additives or preservatives.

Troovy's co-founder & CBO Aditya Mukherjee said, "This backing (investment) is a vote of confidence in a model most food companies don't use: building with the people who'll actually eat what you make. When you build with users, you have to push innovation, because users don't settle. It's not enough to replace the oil and sugar; you have to reduce them dramatically.”

Troovy says it has engaged with over 100 mothers and their children through community-led discussions, recipe brainstorming, and product tastings. These conversations have helped shape the brand’s approach to creating snacks with good ingredients, without harmful preservatives or additives, while maintaining the taste that children expect, the company said.

Ankita Balotia, Principal, Fireside Ventures, said, "Troovy grew 5x in the eight months following our last investment, and that is what made us double down. The team has executed incredibly well on growth, and the backend supply chain.”

Troovy had raised $5 million in a Series A round of funding in January this year.

item.title: Jio Platforms gains 27% on day one of listing, becomes second most valued company in India
item.description: Jio Platforms exceeded market expectations with a 26.81% gain on day one of listing and a market capitalisation of Rs 13 lakh crore.
item.content:encoded:
After making a strong debut on the National Stock Exchange today, the shares of Jio Platforms closed at Rs 1,419, at a gain of 26.81%.

Jio Platforms achieved a market capitalisation of Rs 13,06,761.47 crore on its first day of trading, making it the second most valued company on the Indian stock markets, next only only to its parent firm Reliance Industries.

The top five Indian companies in terms of market capitalisation now are: Reliance Industries (Rs 16 lakh crore), Jio Platforms (Rs 13 lakh crore), Bharti Airtel (Rs 12 lakh crore), HDFC Bank (Rs 10.57 lakh crore), and ICICI Bank (Rs 9.89 lakh crore). Tata Consultancy Services has moved to the sixth place (Rs 8.90 lakh crore).

Jio Platforms' share opened at Rs 1,358 today, gaining 21.3% over the issue price of Rs 1,119 apiece.

The company's Rs 30,213-crore IPO received an overwhelming response from investors last week. It was oversubscribed in less than two hours on opening day, and closed with a 22X oversubscription.

As it positions itself as a technology firm, Jio Platforms is betting on digital services, artificial intelligence, and cloud computing to drive growth beyond telecom.

"There is no either-or at Jio: the network is our technology," said Akash Ambani, Managing Director of Jio Platforms, highlighting the company's in-house 5G core, cloud-native radio access network, and software platform serving 533.3 million customers.

“Connectivity was the first product we built on that platform. Digital services, AI and cloud are what we are layering on top of it now," he said.

Meanwhile, brokerage houses are bullish on the prospects of Jio Platforms.

Motilal Oswal, in its note, said scaling up digital platforms (cloud, enterprise communications, IoT, and managed services, along with international tie-ups for 5G/UBR technology) will offer Jio Platforms the next leg of growth beyond the connectivity business.

The brokerage house has set a bull-case target price of Rs 1,690 crore and a bear-case target price of Rs 1,035.

item.title: Why women should build their front row; AI automation and its impact on jobs
item.description: Kripa Venkatachalam, VP, India Technical Field Organisation & Global Customer Success at Cadence Design Systems, reflects on gender barriers, changing workplace policies, and the importance of having people who cheer you.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

India’s ambition to achieve defence self-reliance gets a big boost. 

Sarvam has inked a five-year agreement with the defence ministry to develop AI tech for the armed forces. The Bengaluru-based AI company will design, develop and deploy AI applications for operations, training, and decision-support, and also provide follow-on technical assistance. The deal envisages shared foundation models, agentic infrastructure, and geospatial and perception systems.

In other news, the high-stakes boardroom battle at the Tata Group continues. 

Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata has challenged the resolution to reappoint N Chandrasekaran as the chairman of Tata Sons. The resolution was passed at the board meeting of the Tata conglomerate’s holding company on September 17.  

According to sources, Noel has called the reappointment “void”, arguing that it was taken out of turn and was not on the meeting’s agenda. 

Meanwhile, as it reshapes its workforce amid heavy AI investments, Microsoft is offering employees an exit option. 

The American tech major has announced a voluntary exit programme for eligible employees in India, the US, the UK, and Canada. The package includes one month’s base salary for each completed year of service, besides health insurance and career transition services. Globally, around 60,000 employees are eligible for the programme. Microsoft has about 23,000 employees in India. However, it’s not clear how many would be eligible in the country. 

Lastly, Wall Street is closely watching the upcoming Big Tech earnings, which could serve as testimony to AI growth in an otherwise turbulent market. 

In today’s newsletter, we will talk about 

  • Why women should build their front row
  • AI automation and its impact on jobs

Here’s your trivia for today: At what temperature do Fahrenheit and Celsius match? (Scroll down for the answer)

Women in Tech

Kripa Venkatachalam of Cadence urges women to build their front row

As part of our Women in Tech series, Kripa Venkatachalam, VP, India Technical Field Organisation & Global Customer Success at Cadence Design Systems, reflects on gender barriers, changing workplace policies, mentorship, and the importance of having people who egg you on.

Her career spanning more than two decades has taken her through diverse roles across companies, including LSI Logic Corporation, Synopsys, GlobalFoundries, and Siemens EDA. Today, as VP, India Technical Field Organisation & Global Customer Success at Cadence Design Systems, she has what she calls a “front-row seat” to how the world’s chips are designed in India.

Key takeaways: 

  • Kripa believes women need to seek support, leverage their network, and not always put the burden on themselves. “You have to make your family work for you, your workplace work for you, your society work for you. You have to lean in and take the help,” she says.
  • At informal forums in Cadence, she often speaks about the need for people, especially women, to create their own front row—people cheering for them. “The front row has to assure you. Organisations and managers have to look closer, look harder, and encourage women forward,” she reiterates. 
  • As she looks ahead, Kripa resists the idea of tying her ambitions to a title. She describes her career as a jungle gym rather than a ladder, an image she credits to Sheryl Sandberg.

Capital no longer creates jobs: Yatish Rajawat of Hundred Million Jobs

At TechSparks 2026, K Yatish Rajawat, Co-founder of Hundred Million Jobs, a non-profit initiative to create 100 million net jobs in India over the next decade, said MSMEs, data laws, entrepreneurship and reskilling will shape the next wave of employment in the country.

Key takeaways: 

  • Rajawat identified three trends reshaping the economy. One, the old formula, wherein Rs 100 crore of investment generates around 10,000 jobs, no longer holds, said Rajawat. Schemes such as the production-linked incentive are tied to capital rather than employment, he added. 
  • The second trend is the impact of AI and automation. AI is already affecting white-collar work across sectors. MSMEs, which he called the country’s largest job engine, are also losing jobs to automation.
  • The third is platform consolidation. Rajawat argued that dominant ecommerce and social media platforms hold consumer data, which new entrepreneurs need, and this kind of monopoly prevents new businesses from succeeding. If entrepreneurship stalls, so does job creation, he said.

item.title: Info Edge reports steady growth; Reimagining everyday consumer products
item.description: Info Edge delivered a steady Q2, with consolidated revenue rising 12.2% year-on-year to Rs 903.9 crore and net profit surging 87% to Rs 649.8 crore.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

Jio Platforms made a strong debut on the National Stock Exchange, closing at Rs 1,419, which is a sharp 26.81% premium over its issue price of Rs 1,119. 

The listing has catapulted the company’s market capitalisation to Rs 13.06 lakh crore, crowning it India’s second most valuable listed firm. It currently trails only its parent, Reliance Industries, and has moved past heavyweights such as Bharti Airtel and TCS. 

The listing day follows a heavily sought-after Rs 30,213-crore IPO, which was fully subscribed within two hours of launch and ultimately closed 22 times oversubscribed.

In other news, PhysicsWallah’s School of Startups (PW SoS) has signed a two-year memorandum of understanding with the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) to support early-stage ventures. The programme, which is expected to focus on Tier-II and III cities and rural areas, combines training and mentoring with prototype development, incubation, investor access and seed capital.

Meanwhile, India wants more women in the workforce, but the numbers tell a different story: female labour force participation sits at 34.6% but the country logged nearly 4.4 lakh crimes against women in a single year. Indian women’s safety is a key barrier to their economic ambitions.

In response, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has issued an advisory across central ministries, Indian Railways, and state administrations. Spanning eight critical fronts, from physical infrastructure and policing to bystander intervention and cyber safety, the message is clear: women’s safety is neither a perk nor merely about physical security. It is an economic imperative and a constitutional right to equal opportunity.
